items.title: kubectl create ingress accepts trailing data in --rule and silently drops TLS

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

items.body:
### What happened?
                                                                                                                           
  kubectl create ingress accepts malformed trailing data in --rule.                                                        
                                                                                                                           
  For example, this malformed rule passes client-side validation:                                                          
                                                                                                                           
  foo.com/=svc:http,tls=secret123,garbage                                                                                  
                                                                                                                           
  The extra ,garbage causes TLS parsing to be skipped. The resulting Ingress has no spec.tls, despite the rule containing  
  tls=secret123.

  This is a client-side validation bug that can silently create an Ingress without the intended TLS configuration.         
                                                                                                                           
  ### What did you expect to happen?                                                                                       
                                                                                                                           
  The command should reject the rule because it does not match the documented format:                                      
                                                                                                                           
  host/path=svcname:svcport[,tls[=secret]]                                                                                 
                                                                                                                           
  For example:                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                           
  rule foo.com/=svc:http,tls=secret123,garbage is invalid and should be in format host/path=svcname:svcport[,tls[=secret]] 
                                                                                                                           
  ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?                                                    
                                                                                                                           
  Run:                                                                                                                     
                                                                                                                           
  $ kubectl create ingress demo \                                                                                          
      --rule='foo.com/=svc:http,tls=secret123,garbage' \                                                                   
      --dry-run=client \                                                                                                   
      -o yaml                                                                                                              
                                                                                                                           
  Expected: the command rejects the malformed rule.                                                                        
                                                                                                                           
  Actual: the command accepts it and renders an Ingress with an HTTP rule but without a spec.tls entry.                    
                                                                                                                           
  The behavior was also reproduced with a focused unit test:                                                               
                                                                                                                           
  CreateIngressOptions{                                                                                                    
      Rules: []string{"foo.com/=svc:http,tls=secret123,garbage"},                                                          
  }.Validate()                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                           
  Validate() returns nil. Constructing the Ingress from those options produces zero TLS rules.                             
                                                                                                                           
  ### Anything else we need to know?                                                                                       
                                                                                                                           
  Root cause:                                                                                                              
                                                                                                                           
  - ruleRegex is anchored at the start but not at the end.                                                                 
  - Validate() uses MatchString, so a valid prefix is sufficient.                                                          
  - buildTLSRules() only processes rules split into exactly two comma-separated fields. The trailing field makes the length
    three, so TLS is skipped.                                                                                              
                                                                                                                           
  Relevant code:                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                           
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create/create_ingress.go#L49   
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create/create_ingress.go#L223  
  - https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/create/create_ingress.go#L326  
                                                                                                                           
  Suggested fix: end-anchor the validation regex and add regression tests for trailing data.                               
                                                                                                                           
  I searched open and closed Kubernetes issues and PRs using command-, symptom-, and file-based queries and did not find an  existing matching report or open fix.                                                                                    
                                                                                                                           
  ### Kubernetes version                                                                                                   
                                                                                                                           
  Client Version: v1.36.2                                                                                                  
  Source tag commit: 24e2b02af5543d7910c2bb074c7264df5a8f0467                                                              
                                                                                                                           
  ### Cloud provider                                                                                                       
                                                                                                                           
  Not applicable. This is a client-side kubectl parsing and validation issue; it does not require a cluster or cloud       
  provider.                                                                                                                
                                                                                                                           
  ### OS version                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                           
  Windows, amd64                                                                                                           
                                                                                                                           
  ### Install tools                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                           
  Built/tested from a local Kubernetes source checkout with Go 1.26.4.                                                     
                                                                                                                           
  ### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)                                                                  
                                                                                                                           
  Not applicable.                                                                                                          
                                                                                                                           
  ### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)                                                         
                                                                                                                           
  Not applicable.

items.title: kubectl explain: add an -o skeleton output format for a copy-pasteable YAML starting point

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

items.body:
cc @kubernetes/sig-cli-feature-requests

## What would you like to be added?

A new `kubectl explain <type> -o skeleton` output format that renders a
resource's schema as a concise, editable YAML skeleton (field names with
placeholder values) instead of the verbose field-by-field prose that
`plaintext`/`plaintext-openapiv2` produce.

A companion `-o skeleton-comments` renders the same skeleton with short
inline `# ...` comments for fields that need explaining: `# required`,
`# enum: A|B|C`, `# map[string]string`, and a drill-down hint for fields
collapsed for depth (see below).

Example, `kubectl explain deployments.spec.template.spec.containers -o skeleton`:

```yaml
containers:
- name: "<required>"
  args:
  - ""
  command:
  - ""
  env: []
  envFrom: []
  image: ""
  imagePullPolicy: ""
  lifecycle: {}
  livenessProbe: {}
  ports: []
  readinessProbe: {}
  resources: {}
  securityContext: {}
  startupProbe: {}
  stdin: false
  stdinOnce: false
  terminationMessagePath: ""
  terminationMessagePolicy: ""
  tty: false
  volumeDevices: []
  volumeMounts: []
  workingDir: ""
```

Design notes:
- Placeholder values come from the schema's own `default`, else the first
  `enum` value, else `example`, else a type-appropriate zero value. A
  required field with none of those (typically a bare string) gets the
  literal `"<required>"` sentinel so it isn't mistaken for an intentionally
  empty optional field.
- The `status` subresource and server-managed `metadata` fields
  (`resourceVersion`, `uid`, `managedFields`, etc.) are omitted, since nobody
  hand-authors those.
- To keep output readable on resources with deep optional structure (Pod's
  `affinity`/`tolerations`/`securityContext`, CRD validation schemas), each
  optional field spends against a small budget before its own optional
  children collapse to a placeholder with a drill-down hint (e.g.
  `# optional, nested further -- see: kubectl explain pods.spec.affinity -o skeleton`).
  Required fields are free, so a load-bearing chain like
  `containers[].image` always expands regardless of depth.
- Implemented as one more template in the existing `pkg/explain/v2`
  template-based generator (same mechanism as `plaintext-openapiv2`), so it
  only touches the openapiv3 explain path.

## Why is this needed?

`kubectl explain` today is documentation-first: it's great for looking up
what a field means, but not for the common case of "I want to write a
Deployment/CRD manifest and need a skeleton to fill in." Today's next-best
alternatives (`kubectl create deployment ... --dry-run=client -o yaml`,
hand-copying from docs, or `explain --recursive`) either only cover a
handful of built-in kinds, produce output flooded with every field
regardless of relevance, or don't work at all for CRDs.

`-o skeleton` gives a fast, copy-pasteable starting point for any resource
the cluster serves an OpenAPI v3 schema for, including CRDs, while staying
short enough to read. The optional-depth budget means you see the fields
that actually need decisions (`containers[].image`) without also seeing
every leaf of `affinity`/`tolerations` you probably don't need today, and
you can always drill into a collapsed field with a normal
`explain <type>.<field> -o skeleton` call.

This is proposed as a proof of concept with a working implementation and
test suite already in hand (unit tests covering required/optional
ordering, enums, maps, `$ref` cycles, field-path drill-down, and the
depth-budget behavior). Happy to open the PR once there's SIG CLI agreement
on the approach/flag naming.

**What happened?**
Three flag descriptions in `kubectl logs` contain typos that appear in `kubectl logs --help` output:

1. `--previous`: "the previous instance of thecontainer" → missing space → should be "the container"
2. `--ignore-errors`: "allow forany errors" → missing space → should be "allow for any errors"  
3. `--since-time`: "(RFC3339).Defaults" → missing period space → should be "(RFC3339). Defaults"

**How to reproduce:**

**Location:**
`staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/logs/logs.go` lines 199, 201, 202

**Fix:**
Correct the three typos in the flag descriptions.

items.title: nil-pointer panic on RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding when kubectl auth reconcile returns an error

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/auth
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Auth.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

items.body:
### What happened?

Argo CD controller crashed when the caller lacks RBAC permission instead of erroring. https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/issues/28607

`kubectl auth reconcile` panics with a nil-pointer dereference when reconciling a
`RoleBinding` or `ClusterRoleBinding` if the underlying reconcile operation returns an
error (e.g. a `forbidden` response because the caller lacks RBAC permissions)

**Proposed fix**: add the same if err != nil { return err } guard after
retry.RetryOnConflict(...) in both the *rbacv1.RoleBinding and
*rbacv1.ClusterRoleBinding cases.


### What did you expect to happen?

`kubectl auth reconcile `should return the underlying error (e.g. the forbidden error)
and exit non-zero, exactly as it does for Role/ClusterRole, instead of panicking.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Reconcile a RoleBinding as a user without permission to get/create it:

```
cat > rb.yaml <<'EOF'
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata:
  name: test-rb
  namespace: default
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: Role
  name: some-role
subjects:
- kind: ServiceAccount
  name: nobody
  namespace: default
EOF
```

kubectl auth reconcile -f rb.yaml --as=system:serviceaccount:default:nobody

Instead of a clean forbidden error, kubectl panics:

```
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x0 pc=...]

k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/auth.(*ReconcileOptions).RunReconcile.func1(...)
        .../pkg/cmd/auth/reconcile.go:274 +0x...
k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/resource.(*DecoratedVisitor).Visit...
k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/resource.ConcurrentVisitorList.Visit.func1()
golang.org/x/sync/errgroup.(*Group).Go.func1()
```

### Anything else we need to know?

introduced in v0.35.0 and still present on master.
v0.34.0 guards all four cases correctly; the retry.RetryOnConflict rewrite that
landed in v0.35.0 added the retry wrapper to the binding cases but omitted the
if err != nil { return err } check that the Role/ClusterRole cases retained.

Found using Argo CD impersonation feature

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
v1.35.0
```

kubectl v1.35.0 through v1.36 and current master

</details>


### Cloud provider

N/A

```console
$ cat /etc/os-release
# paste output here
$ uname -a
# paste output here

# On Windows:
C:\> wmic os get Caption, Version, BuildNumber, OSArchitecture

```

items.title: kubectl: autocomplete --dry-run with '=' and value suggestions (none/server/client)

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

items.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Improve shell completion for the `--dry-run` flag on mutating `kubectl` commands
(`apply`, `create`, `delete`, `patch`, `scale`, …) so that:

- `kubectl apply --dry-run<TAB>` completes to **`--dry-run=`** (with no trailing
  space and no file listing), and
- `kubectl apply --dry-run=<TAB>` suggests the valid values **`none` / `server` /
  `client`**.

**I'm working on this.** There is a cross-repo dependency: `--dry-run` carries an
optional value (it sets `NoOptDefVal` to support the deprecated bare `--dry-run`),
and cobra currently offers no way for a program to make a flag complete as
`--flag=`. I've opened an opt-in enhancement upstream in cobra to enable it:

- spf13/cobra#2433 — adds `Command.MarkFlagAppendEqual`

Once that lands and is vendored, the kubectl side is a small change in
`AddDryRunFlag` (registering value completion for `none/server/client` and
calling `MarkFlagAppendEqual("dry-run")`).

### Why is this needed?

For a flag with `NoOptDefVal` set, the only syntax that actually assigns a value
is `--dry-run=value`; `--dry-run value` (space-separated) treats `value` as a
positional argument and errors. Yet today `kubectl apply --dry-run<TAB>`
completes to `--dry-run ` (with a space) and then offers file completion, which:

- nudges users toward the non-working space-separated form, and
- gives no hint of the valid values (`none`, `server`, `client`).

Guiding users to `--dry-run=client` / `--dry-run=server` via completion makes the
flag more discoverable and steers them away from the deprecated bare `--dry-run`.

/sig cli
/kind feature

items.title: kubectl port-forward: no way to suppress 'Handling connection for' messages

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

labels.name: triage/accepted
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR is ready to be actively worked on.

items.body:
## What happened?

`kubectl port-forward` unconditionally prints "Handling connection for <port>" to stderr on every connection.  There is no flag to suppress these messages.

For long-running tunnels with frequent connections, this produces a constant stream of noise that buries actual errors on the same file descriptor.

## What did you expect to happen?

A `--quiet` or `--verbosity` flag (or gating behind `-v` log levels) so users can suppress informational messages while preserving real errors on stderr.

## How can we reproduce it?

```
kubectl port-forward pod/any-pod 5432:5432
```

Connect to localhost:5432 from another terminal.  Each connection prints:

```
Handling connection for 5432
```

There is no way to disable this without filtering all of stderr, which risks hiding real errors.

## Anything else we need to know?

The message originates from a hardcoded `fmt.Fprintf(o.Out, "Handling connection for %d\n", port)` in `pkg/cmd/portforward/portforward.go` with no verbosity check.

Gating it behind `klog.V(1)` or similar would be sufficient.

## Environment

- kubectl version: client v1.33
- OS: macOS 15 (Darwin 25.5.0)

items.title: kubectl: `cluster-info dump --output-directory` writes pod logs (with embedded secrets) as world-readable

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: sig/cli
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG CLI.

labels.name: sig/security
labels.description: Categorizes an issue or PR as relevant to SIG Security.

labels.name: needs-triage
labels.description: Indicates an issue or PR lacks a `triage/foo` label and requires one.

items.body:
### What happened?

`kubectl cluster-info dump --output-directory=DUMP` writes every dump file via `setupOutputWriter`, which does:

```go
// staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/clusterinfo/clusterinfo_dump.go:126 (func setupOutputWriter)
file, err := os.Create(fullFile)
```

`os.Create` opens files `O_RDWR|O_CREATE|O_TRUNC` with mode `0666` before umask. With the very common `0022` umask that is `0644` (world-readable); with `0002` (common on shared systems / some distros) it is `0664` (group- and other-readable). Parents are created `0755` (`os.MkdirAll(parent, 0755)` at line 124), so the directory tree is traversable by "other".

Pod logs are dumped verbatim to `{DUMP}/{namespace}/{pod}/logs.txt` (line 295 → `writer.Write(data)` at line 287, raw bytes straight from the `log` API). Pod logs routinely contain application secrets: bearer tokens, DB connection strings, cloud credentials, signed URLs, signed certificate/key material, etc.

### What did you expect to happen?

Dump files should be created owner-only (`0600`), and the dump directory tree owner-only (`0700`) when it contains pod logs or other potentially sensitive cluster state, so that an unprivileged local user cannot read the operator's cluster dump.

Preconditions on the victim host: another local user can traverse the path to DUMP (the typical case — DUMP in a home dir, `/tmp`, a shared scratch dir, or a CI artifact dir whose parents are `0755`). The attacker needs **no Kubernetes API credentials at all** — only filesystem read on files kubectl itself just created.

1. Authorized/privileged operator runs kubectl once:
   ```bash
   kubectl cluster-info dump --output-directory=DUMP --all-namespaces
   ```
   kubectl creates DUMP and all nested dirs `0755`, and every `logs.txt` (and `nodes.txt`, `events.txt`, …) `0644`/`0664`, with full pod-log contents — across **all** namespaces requested.
2. A second unprivileged local user reads the logs directly:
   ```bash
   cat $DUMP/*/leaky/logs.txt        # 044-mode readable + traversable parents (0755) => readable by "other"
   ```
   No exploit primitive required — ordinary filesystem ACLs. `--all-namespaces` widens the blast radius to logs from every namespace, including ones the attacker has no RBAC right to read.
3. Extract whatever secret the logs leaked (token, password, cert+key), then use it against the cluster or upstream systems:
   ```bash
   kubectl --token=<LEAKED> ...        # if a bearer token was logged
   # or use a leaked DB connection string / cloud credential against the corresponding backend
   ```
   → access beyond the attacker's normal reach, often as a high-privilege workload identity.

Exposure is **durable**: the files persist at `0644`/`0664` on disk under DUMP until someone manually tightens permissions or deletes them, and re-running the dump re-creates them the same way. On a shared host captured by automation, the window can stay open indefinitely.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run this single self-contained snippet from the root of a Kubernetes checkout. It spins up a fake API server that returns one pod whose `log` endpoint serves a secret marker, then runs the real `kubectl cluster-info dump` and reports the resulting file mode + leak. It uses an already-built `kubectl` (`_output/local/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl` or `_output/bin/kubectl`).

```bash
set -e
KUBECTL="${KUBECTL:-_output/local/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl}"
[ -x "$KUBECTL" ] || KUBECTL=_output/bin/kubectl
[ -x "$KUBECTL" ] || { echo "build kubectl first: make kubectl"; exit 1; }

python3 - "$PWD/$KUBECTL" <<'PY'
import http.server, json, os, pathlib, socket, stat, subprocess, sys, tempfile, threading, urllib.parse
kubectl_bin = sys.argv[1]
secret = "TOKEN=cluster-log-secret-12345\n"
def list_obj(kind, items=None):
    return {"apiVersion": "v1", "kind": kind, "metadata": {"resourceVersion": "1"}, "items": items or []}
def apps_list(kind):
    return {"apiVersion": "apps/v1", "kind": kind, "metadata": {"resourceVersion": "1"}, "items": []}
pod = {"apiVersion": "v1", "kind": "Pod",
       "metadata": {"name": "leaky", "namespace": "default", "uid": "11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111"},
       "spec": {"containers": [{"name": "app", "image": "busybox"}]}, "status": {"phase": "Running"}}

class H(http.server.BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def log_message(self, *a): return
    def send_json(self, obj):
        d = json.dumps(obj).encode()
        self.send_response(200); self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
        self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(d))); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(d)
    def do_GET(self):
        p = urllib.parse.urlparse(self.path).path
        if p == "/api": return self.send_json({"kind": "APIVersions", "versions": ["v1"], "serverAddressByClientCIDRs": []})
        if p == "/api/v1": return self.send_json({"kind": "APIResourceList", "apiVersion": "v1", "groupVersion": "v1", "resources": []})
        if p == "/apis": return self.send_json({"kind": "APIGroupList", "apiVersion": "v1", "groups": [{"name": "apps", "versions": [{"groupVersion": "apps/v1", "version": "v1"}], "preferredVersion": {"groupVersion": "apps/v1", "version": "v1"}}]})
        if p == "/apis/apps/v1": return self.send_json({"kind": "APIResourceList", "apiVersion": "v1", "groupVersion": "apps/v1", "resources": []})
        if p == "/api/v1/nodes": return self.send_json(list_obj("NodeList"))
        if p == "/api/v1/namespaces/default/events": return self.send_json(list_obj("EventList"))
        if p == "/api/v1/namespaces/default/replicationcontrollers": return self.send_json(list_obj("ReplicationControllerList"))
        if p == "/api/v1/namespaces/default/services": return self.send_json(list_obj("ServiceList"))
        if p == "/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods": return self.send_json(list_obj("PodList", [pod]))
        if p == "/apis/apps/v1/namespaces/default/daemonsets": return self.send_json(apps_list("DaemonSetList"))
        if p == "/apis/apps/v1/namespaces/default/deployments": return self.send_json(apps_list("DeploymentList"))
        if p == "/apis/apps/v1/namespaces/default/replicasets": return self.send_json(apps_list("ReplicaSetList"))
        if p == "/api/v1/namespaces/default/pods/leaky/log":
            d = secret.encode(); self.send_response(200); self.send_header("Content-Type", "text/plain")
            self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(d))); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(d); return
        self.send_response(404); self.end_headers(); self.wfile.write(("not found: " + p).encode())

with socket.socket() as s:
    s.bind(("127.0.0.1", 0)); port = s.getsockname()[1]
srv = http.server.ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", port), H)
threading.Thread(target=srv.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()
out = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="cluster-info-dump-poc-"); os.chmod(out, 0o755)
try:
    cmd = [kubectl_bin, f"--server=http://127.0.0.1:{port}", "--kubeconfig=/dev/null",
           "cluster-info", "dump", "--namespaces=default", "--output-directory=" + out, "-o", "json"]
    r = subprocess.run(cmd, text=True, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.PIPE)
    if r.returncode != 0:
        print("ERROR: kubectl cluster-info dump failed", file=sys.stderr)
        print(r.stdout, file=sys.stderr); print(r.stderr, file=sys.stderr); sys.exit(r.returncode)
    lp = pathlib.Path(out) / "default" / "leaky" / "logs.txt"
    content = lp.read_text(); mode = stat.S_IMODE(lp.stat().st_mode)
    print(f"kubectl        : {kubectl_bin}")
    print(f"dump_dir       : {out}")
    print(f"log_file       : {lp}")
    print(f"log_mode       : {mode:04o}")
    print(f"contains_secret: {secret.strip() in content}")
    print(f"other_readable : {bool(mode & 0o004)}")
    if (mode & 0o004) and secret.strip() in content:
        print("VULNERABLE: log dump file is readable by other users and contains the secret marker")
finally:
    srv.shutdown()
PY
```

Expected output (observed; mode depends on umask — `0644` under `0022`, `0664` under `0002`, both other-readable):

```text
kubectl        : .../kubectl
dump_dir       : /tmp/cluster-info-dump-poc-XXXX
log_file       : /tmp/cluster-info-dump-poc-XXXX/default/leaky/logs.txt
log_mode       : 0664
contains_secret: True
other_readable : True
VULNERABLE: log dump file is readable by other users and contains the secret marker
```

The pod log containing the secret marker is written to a mode-`0664` (or `0644`) file readable by other local users. No API binding or real cluster is involved.

### Anything else we need to know?

- Sink: `staging/src/k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/clusterinfo/clusterinfo_dump.go:126`, `func setupOutputWriter`, called from the dump path (e.g. pod logs at line 295; also nodes/events/services/pods/etc.). Parents created `0755` at line 124.
- Same class as the already-reported client-go kubeconfig migration (`0666`→`0644`) and kubeadm/kube-scheduler config writers — sensitive runtime output written `0666` before umask instead of owner-only.
- Suggested fix: create dump files `0600` (`os.OpenFile(fullFile, os.O_WRONLY|os.O_CREATE|os.O_TRUNC, 0600)`) and the dump directory tree `0700` when writing pod logs / sensitive cluster state.

items.body:
### What happened?

`kubectl apply --dry-run=client` fails for existing CRD resources with an error
"applying patch locally: expected a struct, but received a nil". 


### What did you expect to happen?

The command should perform successful dry-run.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Run the following script, which creates a CRD and the tries to perform
an apply with the `--dry-run=client` option:

```
#!/bin/sh
set -x -e

cat > "crd.yaml" << 'EOF'
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: bugs.bug-repro.example.com
spec:
  group: bug-repro.example.com
  names:
    kind: Bug
    plural: bugs
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
EOF

cat > "crd-modified.yaml" << 'EOF'
apiVersion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1
kind: CustomResourceDefinition
metadata:
  name: bugs.bug-repro.example.com
  labels:
    bug-repro: "true"
spec:
  group: bug-repro.example.com
  names:
    kind: Bug
    plural: bugs
  scope: Namespaced
  versions:
  - name: v1
    served: true
    storage: true
    schema:
      openAPIV3Schema:
        type: object
EOF

kubectl apply -f crd.yaml

kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f crd-modified.yaml
```

The output:
```
+ cat
+ cat
+ kubectl apply -f crd.yaml
customresourcedefinition.apiextensions.k8s.io/bugs.bug-repro.example.com created
+ kubectl apply --dry-run=client -f crd-modified.yaml
error: error when applying patch:

to:
Resource: "apiextensions.k8s.io/v1, Resource=customresourcedefinitions", GroupVersionKind: "apiextensions.k8s.io/v1, Kind=CustomResourceDefinition"
Name: "bugs.bug-repro.example.com", Namespace: ""
for: "crd-modified.yaml": applying patch locally: expected a struct, but received a nil
```


### Anything else we need to know?

**Other versions affected**

Reproduces also with kubectl 1.36.0

**An attempt at root cause analysis**

The problem is in 'k8s.io/kubectl/pkg/cmd/apply/patcher.go':

1. PatchLocal is called for --dry-run=client. It calls patchSimple with the localApply=true. (the last argument):

``` 
func (p *Patcher) PatchLocal(current runtime.Object, modified []byte, errOut io.Writer) ([]byte, runtime.Object, error) {
	return p.patchSimple(current, modified, "", "", errOut, true)
}
```

Below is patchSimple(). 

At lines 111 and 136 it determines whether the resource supports StrategicMergePatch using OpenAPI and OpenAPI V3 schemas and tries to produce such a patch. 

CustomResourceDefinition is one of such resource kinds, so it will create a patch and set  `patchType` to StrategicMergePatchType. 

patch!=nil, so it will not enter the block on line 149.

The applied resource differs from the current version ,so patch won't be empty,
so it will continue after the check on line 168.

localApply=true, so it will enter the block at line 171

Here on 174 it will call `scheme.Scheme.New(p.Mapping.GroupVersionKind)`, which will fail because CRD is in 'apiextensions.k8s.io/v1', apiextensions are not  builtin k8s types, so the call will fail. 

The code skips checking error status (probably it assumes (erroneously) that StrategicMerge patch always comes from line 149).

So after ignoring the error it calls `strategicpatch.StrategicMergePatch(current, patch, versionedObj)` with versionedObj==nil.

This call fails with the cryptic error "expected a struct, but received a nil" 


```
 98	func (p *Patcher) patchSimple(obj runtime.Object, modified []byte, namespace, name string, errOut io.Writer, localApply bool) ([]byte, runtime.Object, error) {
    99		// Serialize the current configuration of the object from the server.
   100		current, err := runtime.Encode(unstructured.UnstructuredJSONScheme, obj)
   101		if err != nil {
   102			return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("serializing current configuration from:\n%v\nfor: %w", obj, err)
   103		}
       
   104		// Retrieve the original configuration of the object from the annotation.
   105		original, err := util.GetOriginalConfiguration(obj)
   106		if err != nil {
   107			return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("retrieving original configuration from:\n%v\nfor: %w", obj, err)
   108		}
       
   109		var patchType types.PatchType
   110		var patch []byte
       
   111		if p.OpenAPIV3Root != nil {
   112			gvkSupported, err := p.gvkSupportsPatchOpenAPIV3(p.Mapping.GroupVersionKind)
   113			if err != nil {
   114				// Realistically this error logging is not needed (not present in V2),
   115				// but would help us in debugging if users encounter a problem
   116				// with OpenAPI V3 not present in V2.
   117				klog.V(5).Infof("warning: OpenAPI V3 path does not exist - group: %s, version %s, kind %s\n",
   118					p.Mapping.GroupVersionKind.Group, p.Mapping.GroupVersionKind.Version, p.Mapping.GroupVersionKind.Kind)
   119			} else if gvkSupported {
   120				patch, err = p.buildStrategicMergePatchFromOpenAPIV3(original, modified, current)
   121				if err != nil {
   122					// Fall back to OpenAPI V2 if there is a problem
   123					// We should remove the fallback in the future,
   124					// but for the first release it might be beneficial
   125					// to fall back to OpenAPI V2 while logging the error
   126					// and seeing if we get any bug reports.
   127					fmt.Fprintf(errOut, "warning: error calculating patch from openapi v3 spec: %v\n", err)
   128				} else {
   129					patchType = types.StrategicMergePatchType
   130				}
   131			} else {
   132				klog.V(5).Infof("warning: OpenAPI V3 path does not support strategic merge patch - group: %s, version %s, kind %s\n",
   133					p.Mapping.GroupVersionKind.Group, p.Mapping.GroupVersionKind.Version, p.Mapping.GroupVersionKind.Kind)
   134			}
   135		}
       
   136		if patch == nil && p.OpenAPIGetter != nil {
   137			if openAPISchema, err := p.OpenAPIGetter.OpenAPISchema(); err == nil && openAPISchema != nil {
   138				// if openapischema is used, we'll try to get required patch type for this GVK from Open API.
   139				// if it fails or could not find any patch type, fall back to baked-in patch type determination.
   140				if patchType, err = p.getPatchTypeFromOpenAPI(openAPISchema, p.Mapping.GroupVersionKind); err == nil && patchType == types.StrategicMergePatchType {
   141					patch, err = p.buildStrategicMergeFromOpenAPI(openAPISchema, original, modified, current)
   142					if err != nil {
   143						// Warn user about problem and continue strategic merge patching using builtin types.
   144						fmt.Fprintf(errOut, "warning: error calculating patch from openapi spec: %v\n", err)
   145					}
   146				}
   147			}
   148		}
       
   149		if patch == nil {
   150			versionedObj, err := scheme.Scheme.New(p.Mapping.GroupVersionKind)
   151			if err == nil {
   152				patchType = types.StrategicMergePatchType
   153				patch, err = p.buildStrategicMergeFromBuiltins(versionedObj, original, modified, current)
   154				if err != nil {
   155					return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf(createPatchErrFormat, original, modified, current, err)
   156				}
   157			} else {
   158				if !runtime.IsNotRegisteredError(err) {
   159					return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("getting instance of versioned object for %v: %w", p.Mapping.GroupVersionKind, err)
   160				}
       
   161				patchType = types.MergePatchType
   162				patch, err = p.buildMergePatch(original, modified, current)
   163				if err != nil {
   164					return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf(createPatchErrFormat, original, modified, current, err)
   165				}
   166			}
   167		}
       
   168		if string(patch) == "{}" {
   169			return patch, obj, nil
   170		}
       
   171		if localApply {
   172			var patchedBytes []byte
   173			if patchType == types.StrategicMergePatchType {
   174				versionedObj, _ := scheme.Scheme.New(p.Mapping.GroupVersionKind)
   175				patchedBytes, err = strategicpatch.StrategicMergePatch(current, patch, versionedObj)
   176			} else {
   177				patchedBytes, err = jsonpatch.MergePatch(current, patch)
   178			}
   179			if err != nil {
   180				return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("applying patch locally: %w", err)
   181			}
   182			patchedObj, _, err := unstructured.UnstructuredJSONScheme.Decode(patchedBytes, nil, nil)
   183			if err != nil {
   184				return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("decoding locally patched object: %w", err)
   185			}
   186			return patch, patchedObj, nil
   187		}

```

items.body:
### What happened?

Bug description
kubectl cp fails on large files and leaving hanging tar zombie process inside the pod 
Scenario:
1. create a pod in k8s with attached pvc - or even with temporary file system.
2. create a large file of several GB inside the pod.
3. copy the pod from inside the pod to a target location where space is lacking.
4. the kubectl cp uses tar inside the pod and will fail due to not enough space.
5. the tar file will be hanging inside the pod .
6. file handle pointing to the file will stay 
7. If using pvc of cephfs - if somone deletes the file , the system does not see it but the cephfs has a stray file
which will never be released till the tar process will be killed or the pod will be terminating -> e.g: killing the tar file

the scenario will eventually cause a "leak" in ceph fs , and might consume all cluster data 
in case this scenario repeats it self during repeated timer 



### What did you expect to happen?

the tar file will be terminated upon failure due to lack of space in target path of copy

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

kubectl cp fails on large files and leaving hanging tar zombie process inside the pod 
Scenario:
1. create a pod in k8s with attached pvc - or even with temporary file system.
2. create a large file of several GB inside the pod.
3. copy the pod from inside the pod to a target location where space is lacking.
4. the kubectl cp uses tar inside the pod and will fail due to not enough space.
5. the tar file will be hanging inside the pod .
6. file handle pointing to the file will stay 
7. If using pvc of cephfs - if somone deletes the file , the system does not see it but the cephfs has a stray file
which will never be released till the tar process will be killed or the pod will be terminating -> e.g: killing the tar file

the scenario will eventually cause a "leak" in ceph fs , and might consume all cluster data 
in case this scenario repeats it self during repeated timer
